items.question: We are about to tender USD 20m of rural road rehabilitation works in Kenya. What should we plan for?

kept.text: Expect the tendering process to take about 252 days on average (p50) with a possible range from 101 days (p10) to 630 days (p90).
The rebid probability is 14.2 %, so budget for a possible re‑tender should be included.
Comparable contracts show a median award time of 189 days and 60 % rebid rate, indicating that delays and re‑tendering are common in Kenya civil‑works procurements.
High staff turnover at the urban (and likely sub‑national) level caused implementation delays; ensure continuity of procurement and project staff or have rapid onboarding plans.
Provide timely capacity‑building modalities for the national‑scale program; early training reduces bottlenecks.
Set up systems for continuous, reliable monitoring of work progress so the government can intervene quickly when delays appear.
Include continuous training and capacity development for reporting, financial management and environmental/social compliance to avoid compliance gaps.
Publish all tender documents, invitation for bids and award details on the project website as required by the PAD guidelines.
Choose the appropriate bidding method (ICB or NCB) based on thresholds and ensure standard tender documents are up‑to‑date with new regulations.

removed.text: Planning tip: Allocate extra time and resources for staff continuity, capacity building, and robust monitoring to mitigate the high likelihood of delays and rebids observed in similar Kenyan road works.

items.question: What lessons do completion reports give about land acquisition and right-of-way delays in works contracts?

kept.text: Identify all land‑acquisition steps early and try to complete them before project approval; assess the likelihood of timely completion and have fallback options if acquisition stalls.
Do not approve financing when land acquisition is incomplete; unfinished acquisition can halt key activities, as seen when a university could not proceed and withdrew.
Expect land‑acquisition and resettlement to be the biggest implementation challenge; mismatches between government and Bank policies create confusion and delay.
Delayed acquisition often stems from poor preparation, lack of policy harmonization, insufficient agency resources, and limited time allocated during the preparation phase.
Land‑price inflation can dramatically increase costs, forcing implementing agencies to update valuations frequently and adding further delays.
Projects without any land‑acquisition component (e.g., Ghana PSRRP) avoid these risks altogether.

items.question: Have cost estimates been unrealistic compared with bid prices, and what did projects learn from it?

kept.text: Vietnam – Project P160162 – The project underestimated the amount of land needed and its cost, which threatened the scale and quality of the infrastructure.
It learned that cost‑estimate preparation must be tightly overseen, that consultants should be paid for accuracy, and that independent monitoring of consultants is essential
Ghana – Project P164603 – Contracts lacked price‑adjustment terms, so when unforeseen cost changes occurred the project faced cancellations and delays.
The follow‑on project added price‑adjustment clauses to avoid this problem
Ghana – Project P164211 – Rigid budgets left the project vulnerable to inflation and pandemic‑related cost spikes.
The lesson was to build flexible budget planning and contingency reserves from the start
Ghana – Project P152670 – Although the offshore development’s original estimate was US$7.9 billion, efficient industry practice delivered the work about 6 % cheaper (≈US$500 million).
The project highlighted that realistic appraisal estimates combined with strong procurement discipline can produce lower‑than‑expected final costs

removed.text: Overall, projects found that unrealistic cost estimates lead to scope, quality, and schedule risks.
Key remedies are stronger oversight of estimates, payment incentives for accuracy, independent monitoring, inclusion of price‑adjustment clauses, and flexible budgeting with contingency reserves.

items.question: What happened when tenders attracted few bidders, and how did projects respond?
